p: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.

The article gives Mahendravarman I as '571-630 CE' without saying whether these are life or reign; left out.
